title: Jude and Moss's Big Breath Race
markdown:
Jude’s mind was a tinkerer’s delight, full of little gears and pulleys that clicked and whirred, always trying to understand the why of things. He would spend hours watching ants march in perfect lines, or figuring out how a dandelion seed could travel so far on the breeze. Moss the badger stood beside him, fur as brown and soft as a freshly tilled field after spring rain, steady as the oldest oak in the Whispering Woods, always ready with a kind word or a helping paw.

One sun-drenched afternoon they stood at the bottom of Whispering Hill. Not enormous, but steep, grass tickling the bellies of clouds.

“Race you to the top, Moss!” Jude’s eyes were dewdrops in sun. His heart was already thrumming.

Moss looked up from a mushroom worth inspecting. White teeth, twitching whiskers. “You’re on. May the swiftest badger — or boy — win.”

They set off with a burst of energy, a whirlwind of bare legs and sturdy paws. Jude pumped his arms with all his might. Moss’s short powerful legs churned like little pistons. The wind whipped past Jude’s ears. Moss’s fur rippled like a chocolate-coloured flag. But after only a few minutes their legs felt heavy, as if they were wading through thick treacle. Chests thumped like frantic drums. They found themselves panting. Haff, haff, haff. Jude gasped, leaning against a mossy rock that felt cool and damp beneath his sweaty palm. Moss slumped beside him, usually perky whiskers drooping. The scent of crushed grass mingled with their laboured breaths.

“I didn’t know the hill was so tiring,” Moss rasped. “My paws have each carried a boulder.”

Jude’s face was cherry. Muscles like wet noodles. “My whole body feels weak. As if it’s run out of something fizzy and important.” Another ragged breath. Not enough.

Ms. Imani’s voice arrived warm as new bread. She moved without much fussing of leaves, a reed basket smelling of dried herbs and sunshine, eyes crinkling into crescent moons.

“Having a bit of trouble catching your breath?”

“We raced,” Jude said, relief in it. “We got so out of breath we could barely move. As if my body stopped, even though I was trying.”

A soft chuckle, tiny bells. “When you put your body to work, it needs a special kind of fuel. Come. We’ll find what it is, and how to get more.”

She led them away from the steep incline toward a quiet meadow nestled in a gentle dip. It was bathed in warm golden afternoon, humming with life. A little stream gurgled, water sparkling like scattered diamonds. Iridescent butterflies danced on purple clover, sunny buttercups, delicate bluebells. Ms. Imani sat on a soft patch of clover, sweet scent ticking their noses. “Watch,” she said, a gentle invitation.

They watched a busy robin hopping, tiny chest puffing in and out with each dart. Then a plump bumblebee buzzed past, fuzzy abdomen seeming to rise and fall with each powerful wingbeat, a tiny vibrating engine. Even the tall grasses at the meadow’s edge swayed as if breathing the caressing breeze, stalks bowing and rising.

“Everything that moves, everything alive, breathes. That is how they keep going. Now your own chests. Feel what’s happening.”

Jude and Moss set hands over hearts. Not the frantic pant. A slow rise, a fall. In, and out. Air moving.

“When you run,” Ms. Imani said, “your muscles need lots of little helpers. They come from the air. Your lungs are soft balloons tucked inside. Breathe in: they fill. That air gives you the oomph to jump, play, climb a hill.”

Jude’s eyes lit like small lamps. “On the hill we weren’t getting enough oomph-air into the balloons?”

“Precisely. Deep and steady. Fill them. Like sails catching wind.”

They thanked Ms. Imani, hearts lighter from understanding as much as from rest, and walked back to Whispering Hill. This time they did not race. They walked side by side, paying close attention. In, and out. They felt the air fill their chests, a quiet powerful sensation spreading calm strength. They noticed the chirping of a distant cricket, cheerful and rhythmic, and the gentle rustle of leaves as a soft breeze stirred the branches. The world felt richer, more alive, more connected, because they were not gasping past it.

At the top they were not wrecked. Happy. Invigorated. Fields rolled toward a sun that was painting gold and amber, long shadows dancing. The view did the talking.

“It’s so much easier when you breathe right,” Jude said. “It feels good.”

Moss nodded. “As if the air is helping us climb.”

Ms. Imani had followed, a comforting shadow, and stood with them. She did not call the air magic, or the lungs little engines in a closing hymn. She named what they had used: air, all around, invisible, taken in by lungs that work like bellows if you let them fill.

They walked down hand in paw, last light on their faces. Jude timed his steps to his breath, which is a tinkerer’s sort of race, and Moss, who had inspected the mushroom and the hill and the robin, decided all three had been worth the afternoon. Tomorrow they might race again. They would start with a breath that went all the way down.
